job: Oil pressure sensor or switch replacement
unit: One engine oil pressure sensor (also sold as an oil pressure switch or sending unit), fitted, with stored codes cleared. Not included: diagnosis of the oil light, gauge reading or code, a mechanical oil pressure test, an oil and filter change, intake manifold gaskets or seals on engines where the manifold comes off to reach the sensor, wiring or connector repair, and the separate valve-timing (rocker arm) oil pressure switch some engines also carry.

benchmarks.name: Jerry
benchmarks.note: Page states an oil pressure sensor replacement 'can cost $175-$219', part $9-$53, labor rates $85-$150+ an hour, job time 0.5-1.5 hours; page says updated Nov 18, 2026. Its own table of modeled examples for older vehicles (2004 GMC Sierra 1500, 2006 Honda Pilot, 2007 GMC Yukon and others) runs lower, $109.06-$186.87, on 55 or 65 minutes of labor

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. Built totals (part + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), for one sensor or switch: economy 2014 Dodge Dart 2.0L/2.4L about $88-$162 (0.5 hr); midsize 2016 Kia Sorento 3.3L V6 about $201-$268 (1.6 man-hours; the switch itself is under $13); truck 2014 Ram 1500 about $107-$407 (0.4 hr on the 5.7L V8 up to a seller's 2 hours; Chrysler's own time for the 3.6L V6 is 1.6 hr); large near-luxury 2014 Chrysler 300 about $143-$279 (0.7 hr on the 5.7L V8, 1.2 hr on the 3.6L V6). A supportable range is therefore roughly $90-$410, and where the sensor sits decides most of it: the part is cheap and the labor is not. Against the benchmarks, now three publishers: RepairPal ($207-$261) and Jerry ($175-$219) both fall in the middle of the built totals, and YourMechanic's vehicle pages ($182-$517) cover the same span and run higher at the top; its $517 for a 2013 Wrangler 3.6L is well above what Chrysler's warranty time for that engine family would build. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly. Three classes (economy, truck, luxury) rest on one Chrysler bulletin that names the example vehicles and prints the operation as 'Sensor, Oil Pressure - Replace' with times in hours: 0.5 on the Dart, 0.4 and 1.6 on the Ram 1500, 0.7 and 1.2 on the 300. The midsize class now rests on a different maker: Kia's bulletin for the 2016-2018 Sorento 3.3L prints 'Oil Pressure Switch (OPS) Replacement' at 1.6 M/H, with the leak inspection as a separate 0.3 M/H operation. All of these are real maker times for the example vehicles with diagnosis or inspection kept separate, but they are warranty times, the low end of what a shop bills, and for the economy and midsize classes no second stated time was found, so those labor ranges are a single point and a real quote will usually be somewhat higher. The truck high end is a parts seller's approximate 2-hour figure. The luxury class is still the weakest fit and is not resolved: the example is a near-luxury sedan, not a luxury-brand car, because no luxury-brand bulletin was found that prints a standalone sensor replacement time in hours. What was found for luxury brands is shown as cross-checks only: Cadillac (ATS and CTS four-cylinder) prints 'Add Time Replace oil pressure sensor 3.0 Hrs.', but only as an add-on to a wiring repair; BMW prints 'Replacing the oil pressure sensor' at 8 to 10 flat rate units on the 2024 X5 and X7 and 13 to 15 on the 7 Series, which another BMW bulletin implies is 0.8 to 1.5 hours without defining the unit outright; Acura prints 0.3 and 0.4 for the engine oil pressure switch with no unit, read from a forum copy. Taken together they suggest a luxury-brand quote can sit anywhere from below the 300 (an easy-to-reach switch) to well above it (three hours of labor on the Cadillac four-cylinder), so treat the luxury figure as a rough guide. Sensor location: the same Mopar sensor takes 0.4 hr on the Ram 5.7L V8 and 1.6 hr on the Ram 3.6L V6, where the bulletin lists intake plenum and intake manifold seals; Kia allows 1.6-1.8 man-hours on its 3.3L V6, where intake gaskets are replaced with the switch. Chevrolet Silverado, GMC Sierra and Tahoe 5.3L V8: on the 2007-2013 generation the sensor sits at the back of the engine behind the intake manifold, close to the firewall, and some shops remove the intake to reach it, so it costs more labor than an easy-access sensor. That statement rests on weak sources (an owners' forum thread on a 2008 Tahoe 5.3L and a parts seller's guide); no General Motors page stating the Silverado location was loaded, and no maker time for it was found. The General Motors truck bulletins loaded either name an 'Engine Oil Pressure Sensor Replacement' operation and print 'use published time' instead of a figure, or deal with the oil pump, the valve lifter oil filter or wiring instead of the sensor; one (PIP5932D, 1.2L Encore GX, Envista, Trailblazer and Trax) says the sensor is reached by removing the intake manifold. Expect a Silverado quote toward the upper part of the truck range or above it. Parts: genuine list prices are from dealer catalog pages ($81.70 for the Dart sensor, $12.45 for the Sorento switch, $86.70 for the sensor shared by the Ram 1500 and 300). Only the Dart low end is a new aftermarket part ($28.27, on a page that lists the Dart without model years). For the Sorento the low end is the genuine switch at a dealer's discounted online price ($8.70, stated new); the one new aftermarket switch found ($13.20) costs slightly more than the genuine list price and is matched by part number only. For the Ram and 300 the aftermarket prices found ($34.19 and $44.99) were on pages that did not say new, so the low end is the genuine sensor at a dealer's discounted online price ($58.50); the Ram catalog page is for the 2015 model year with the same part number the bulletin names. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, and many shops confirm real oil pressure with a mechanical gauge before replacing the sensor, billed separately. Where the intake manifold comes off to reach the sensor (the Chrysler 3.6L and 3.2L V6, some General Motors V8 trucks, the Kia 3.3L V6), new intake manifold gaskets or seals are added. Also common: an oil and filter change or an oil top-up, a new connector or wiring repair when the plug is oil-soaked, a sensor screen or filter on engines that have one, shop supplies and sales tax. Some engines carry a second, separate oil pressure switch for the valve timing system, quoted on its own.
held_reason: Held at review after one attempt: every class is a Chrysler-family vehicle on one bulletin, the luxury example (Chrysler 300) is not a luxury make, and benchmarks are short of three publishers. Needs a luxury-make example with a maker time printed with a unit.
